- **The shard.** Built and measured: 11m37s -> **~10m**, not the 7m20s predicted. See below.

## The shard, and why it was replaced

First attempt: split CT by runtime across four parallel jobs. It worked and was not enough. `ct-slow` alone measured **8m18s** against the 5m55s extrapolated from the prior run, and both halves pay a 1m23s pinned-toolchain build.

Then the premise evaporated. Once a pull request stops running the slow tier at all, that tier cannot be a PR's critical path -- so splitting `main`'s single run buys nothing a PR benefits from and costs a second job. Replaced by a **tier**.

## What it is now

| | pull request | main / manual dispatch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gate` | `just check-fast` -- lint, 940 eunit, 100 CT | `just check` -- lint, doc, 940 eunit, 223 CT |
| `compat` | 940 eunit, 100 CT, dialyzer | 940 eunit, 223 CT, dialyzer |

`just check-fast` measured **56s** here. **Estimated** ~3m30s on a runner, mostly the 1m23s toolchain build -- the CI run is the measurement.

Dialyzer stays on both tiers: it analyses source, not tests, so its answer does not depend on the CT tier, and 49s is not worth a tier boundary.

**The cost, stated rather than implied.** A PR that breaks SAM, streaming, addressbook, reseed, netdb-srv or a peer-lifecycle suite can go green and turn main red. Real, and chosen: the alternative was a ten-minute signal on every push. Wiring `just check` onto `pull_request` reverses it in one line.

## No i2pd in CI, and now it cannot get there by accident

`apps/i2per/interop/i2p_i2pd_interop_SUITE` boots a **live i2pd** on a routable network. It has never run in CI -- rebar3 only discovers suites in `test/` directories and it sits in `interop/` -- and it is in zero tiers.

That was one glob detail away from changing, since the partition is built by `find`. Now asserted: `ct-suites.sh` refuses to emit any suite matching `interop|i2pd`. **The guard was tested by widening the glob back to `*_SUITE.erl`** -- it fails, naming the offending suite. `just interop` stays a local recipe, deliberately not a CI job and deliberately not `workflow_dispatch`, because a suite that needs the network is a suite whose failure means nothing when the network is what broke.

## One source of truth

`scripts/ct-suites.sh` names the suites for `fast`, `rest`, `slow`, `all`, and is called by both the justfile and the workflow. `rest`/`all` are derived from the tree so a new suite is covered without editing a list; only `fast`/`slow` are explicit, because choosing what runs on every PR should be reviewable. Every named suite is asserted to exist, so a rename fails loudly instead of quietly running one fewer.

`fast` deliberately overlaps `slow` on `i2p_ssu2_handshake_SUITE` -- the handshake without the 22,000-datagram case is exactly what a PR needs. The tiers never run on the same event, so nothing runs twice. `fast` is a subset of `all` but **not** of `rest`, and that is written down rather than assumed.

## Verified locally

- PR tier: `just check-fast` **56s** -- erlfmt clean, 940 eunit, 100 CT
- Main tier: `just check` **223s** -- erlfmt clean, 940 eunit, 223 CT; dialyzer exit 0
- Tier logic: pull_request -> fast (6), push -> all (25), workflow_dispatch -> all (25)
- `rest` + `slow` == `all` == the 25 suites rebar3 actually ran in the CI log

## Next target if it needs to go faster

The 1m23s pinned-toolchain build is now the largest fixed cost on a PR. Caching the devenv profile across runs, or dropping `erlfmt` from the compat job's setup, is where the next few minutes are -- not the tests.

add.issue.name: Three of the four pinned GitHub Actions were behind, and one of them runs on the retiring node20

edit.description.md:
Audited the four actions `gate.yml` pins against upstream releases rather than assuming they were current.

## What was pinned vs what exists

| action | was | now | gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `actions/checkout` | v4 | **v7.0.1** | 3 majors |
| `cachix/install-nix-action` | v27 | **v31.11.1** | 4 majors |
| `cachix/cachix-action` | v15 | **v17** | 2 majors |
| `erlef/setup-beam` | v1 | v1.24.1 | **none -- `@v1` is a floating major tag** |

## One of these was not housekeeping

`cachix/cachix-action` v15 runs on **node20**, which GitHub is retiring. v17 is node24.

That matters more than a version number usually would: `cachix-action` is the step that **populates the devenv cache**. When it breaks, the failure mode is not a red X on one job -- it is a 1m+ rebuild of the pinned toolchain on every run, which is the largest fixed cost on a PR (#B1X7BRK).

## Verified it was a safe bump, not a hopeful one

- **`cachix-action` v15 -> v17**: inputs diffed in full. Same 12 inputs, same defaults, including `skipPush: false` and `useDaemon: true`. The `name` description had been reworded from "push and pull" to "pull and optionally push", which looked like a flipped default -- it is not, the defaults are untouched and only the prose changed. Runtime is the only real difference.
- **`install-nix-action` v27 -> v31**: one input added (`set_as_trusted_user`). `extra_nix_config`, the only thing this workflow passes, is still there.
- **`checkout` v5** -> node24, min runner v2.327.1 (`ubuntu-latest` long past it). **v6** persists credentials to a separate file -- this workflow uses `permissions: contents: read` and never pushes from CI. **v7** blocks fork checkouts under `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`; this workflow triggers on plain `pull_request`, so it does not apply.
- **`setup-beam`** deliberately left at `@v1`, because that tag floats and is already on the newest 1.x. Pinning it to a specific version would be a downgrade in intent.

## Verified

Every pin resolves and ships an `action.yml` at that tag (HTTP 200), checked the way Actions resolves it:

    actions/checkout       v7   200  node24
    cachix/install-nix-action v31 200  composite
    cachix/cachix-action   v17  200  node24
    erlef/setup-beam       v1   200  node24

**No node20 pin remains.** The workflow YAML parses.

## Not claimed

That CI is green with the new majors. Three of these are major bumps, and a major bump of a build action is exactly the kind of change that looks fine in review and fails on a runner -- `checkout` v6's credential change and `cachix` v16/v17's reorganised internals are the plausible candidates. The CI run on the branch is the test, not this reasoning.

add.issue.name: A PropEr generator set the cost of its own property by lottery, and the size limit it was approximating had no test

edit.description.md:
Run `36966857385`. **Not caused by #W6TPY2Y** -- the run before it (`36966136645`) passed the same eunit. This is a latent flake that happened to land here, and it is the same class of defect as #EPZTFX8.

## What failed

```
compat (OTP 28, warnings relaxed)  eunit
  i2p_framing_prop_tests: frame_roundtrip_prop_test...*timed out*
  in function proper_gen:clean_instance_list/1
  Failed: 0.  Skipped: 0.  Passed: 816.
  One or more tests were cancelled.
```

04:59:04 -> 04:59:09: **5.08s**, against eunit's default 5-second per-test budget. 816 of 940 ran before the cancellation.

## The generator was a lottery

```erlang
payload_gen() ->
    ?LET(Size, integer(0, 65519), binary(Size)).      %% up to 64 KB
```

`frame_roundtrip_prop_test` ran **100 draws**, each sealing and opening a payload of up to 64 KB. So the cost of the property was decided by a random draw rather than by the property.

Measured, 8 local runs of the module before the fix: **1.33s to 2.77s** -- a 2x spread -- against a 5s budget. On a runner already running ~2.5x slower than this hardware, the budget is straddled routinely. That is why it passed one run and failed the next.

`blocks_roundtrip_prop_test` had the same shape one level up: `list(block_gen())` puts **no ceiling on the list's length**, so a single draw could exceed the whole run's budget.

## The wide range was buying nothing

Round-tripping at 64 KB and at 4 KB are the same code path. Worse, the generator topped out *at* the limit:

- a random draw could **never exceed** 65519, so `encrypt_frame/4`'s guard clause `when byte_size(Payload) > ?MAX_PAYLOAD -> error({too_large, N})` had **no test at all**;
- and reaching 65519 exactly by uniform draw is a 1-in-65520 chance per test.

So 100 draws of up to 64 KB were spent approximating a boundary they would essentially never hit. **The guard clause -- the easiest line in the file to break -- was untested, and the test was slow anyway.**

## The fix

- `payload_gen()` bounded to 2048, which still crosses the NTCP2 data-packet boundary so single- and multi-packet payloads are both generated. `numtests` unchanged at 100.
- `list(block_gen())` replaced by a bounded `vector(N, block_gen())`, N <= 32.
- **The limits are now stated, deterministically**, replacing what the lottery only approximated:
  - `largest_legal_payload_roundtrips_test` -- exactly 65519 round-trips
  - `one_byte_over_the_limit_is_refused_test` -- 65520 raises `{too_large, 65520}`
  - `empty_payload_roundtrips_test` -- zero-length payload
- A `{timeout, 60, ...}` backstop on all nine tests, so a slow runner cannot turn a bounded property back into a 5-second lottery.

**Coverage went up, not down.** The three new cases test a rejection clause that had none.

## Verified locally

- Module before: **1.33-2.77s** over 8 runs. After: **0.71-0.84s** over 5 runs. The spread collapsed, which is the point -- the cost is now set by the property rather than by a draw.
- **6 tests -> 9**, all passing. The three boundary cases are named in the run output.

## Why the number 65519 is written out

Rather than importing `i2p_framing`'s `?MAX_PAYLOAD`. These are the numbers the specification states; if the constant moves, these tests fail, and a changed protocol limit should arrive as a reviewable diff rather than as a quietly retuned generator.

## Remaining unknowns

- **Why the runner is >11x slower on this specific test** (0.43s here vs >5s there) when the rest of CT is ~2.5x. Not explained. Bounding the generator removes the exposure either way, but the asymmetry itself is unexplained and may affect other tests.
- The other two PropEr modules were checked and are bounded -- `i2p_siphash_prop_tests` tops out at `integer(1, 1024)`, `i2p_ecies_prop_tests` is `binary(32)`. Neither was changed.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Solution: the cap has never held — `global:trans/2` is a shared lock, not a mutex

This is a **correctness fix, not a latency change**, and the re-diagnosis is the substance of the work.

### `global:trans/2` is not a mutex

The ticket (and I, on first read) treated `global:trans/2` as a working lock that cost too much. Between processes sharing an id it is not a lock at all. `m:global:set_lock/3` documents this:

> The global name server keeps track of all processes sharing the same lock, that is, if two processes set the same lock, both processes must delete the lock.

A lock id is `{ResourceId, LockRequesterId}` and the name server matches on the **pair**: `can_set_lock/1` answers "held" for a matching pair, and `insert_lock/4` then *adds* the second process to the holder list and answers `true`. Twelve dialers on one id all run the body.

It only *looks* exclusive when the critical section is short, because `set_lock/4` waits by retrying through `random_sleep/1` — so a loser returns while the holder is still inside, and is granted the lock then. Measured here, OTP 28, twelve processes on one id:

| body of `Fun()` | most processes inside at once |
|---|---|
| returns immediately | 1 |
| sleeps 2 ms | 12 |
| sleeps 20 ms | 12 |

The real body is `which_children/1` plus `start_child/2` — milliseconds.

### Demonstrated red, on the real code

Reverting only the three `start_*` bodies to the `global:trans` shape, cap 4 and 24 dials released from a barrier:

```
ntcp2_cap_holds_under_concurrent_dials_test   expected {ntcp2_cap,4}  got {ntcp2_cap,8}
ssu2_cap_holds_under_concurrent_dials_test    expected {ssu2_cap,4}   got {ssu2_cap,10}
sam_cap_holds_under_concurrent_dials_test     expected {sam_cap,4}    got {sam_cap,24}
```

A second run gave 10, 17 and 24. The number moves because nothing is synchronising it — that is the finding.

So all three caps were **advisory** on exactly the paths this ticket names: a post-restart peer-set rebuild, a floodfill replication burst. The ticket's other two arguments (a cluster-wide lock over a per-node number, randomised back-off) are real and are in the module doc, but they are second-order.

Continues in a second comment.

add.issue.comment.md:
### What landed

A new `i2p_admission` gen_server, one instance per resource, a `permanent` child of the very supervisor whose children it admits. The count and the `supervisor:start_child/2` are one reduction of one process, so no second admission can read a count the first has acted on.

It holds **no state**, which is what makes it hold: the count is read from the supervisor, the only thing that knows what is alive and the only thing this process can add to. No second copy to fall out of step, and a restart is free rather than needing a reconcile. `an_admission_process_is_restarted_after_dying_test` kills it and re-runs the whole cap case against the replacement.

- **`*_limit_reached/0` removed** from all three supervisors. It was the other half of the count-then-start, exported, and a caller reaching for it would reintroduce the race by hand. The count and limit reads stay — admission uses the same ones, so there is one number rather than two.
- **One instance per resource**, which answers the ticket's open question. A SAM session is a connection an operator waits on by hand; the peer caps exist for replication bursts. Three instances, three mailboxes, no queueing between them. Pinned by `the_three_caps_are_independent_test`.
- **SAM's cap counts children now, not ETS rows.** A session writes its registry row *after* `start_child` returns, so a row-based count is a later and smaller number and a session mid-registration counted against nothing. Children are what the limit bounds, and it is also what lets one case pin all three.
- **Three counters**, charged in `i2p_admission` where the cap lives: `ntcp2_connections_refused_limit`, `ssu2_sessions_refused_limit`, `sam_sessions_refused_limit`. A cap being hit was invisible — indistinguishable from a peer refusing us, a NetDb with no address, or a handshake that failed. Counters not events, for the `transit_frames_dropped_no_route` reason: at the cap this fires on every inbound accept and every reconnect attempt, so it is a rate to watch.

### Gate

erlfmt clean, dialyzer clean, **951 eunit** (+8), **223 CT** (unchanged), `just doc` builds. Re-run on the final tree after the last doc edits, not quoted from the previous pass.

### What one of these cases does *not* catch

`admission_does_not_consult_a_cluster_wide_lock_test` takes the three old lock ids and asserts admission is unaffected — and **it passes against the old code too**, because that lock was shared, so holding the id blocked nobody. It catches the lock returning in *exclusive* form (a per-process `LockRequesterId`, or `global:register_name/3` used as a mutex), which is the shape a well-meaning fix for this bug would take. The three cap cases are what pin the property; that one is a guard on the wrong half of the fork and says so in its own comment.

add.issue.name: Streaming connections are the one client-facing kind with no cap at all

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## The gap

`m:i2p_sam_sup:start_stream_conn/1` is the **fourth** client-facing connection kind, and it is the only one with no cap at all. #41D5PFF covered NTCP2 connections, SSU2 sessions and SAM sessions; this one is a bare `supervisor:start_child/2`.

Every `m:i2p_stream_conn` holds a TCP socket to a remote peer, a send window, a receive window and a demux ETS row. Nothing bounds how many exist.

## Who can create them

- `m:i2p_sam_session` — twice, for a STREAM FORWARD accept and for a STREAM ACCEPT
- `m:i2p_server_tunnel` — for an inbound tunnel's accepted streams
- `m:i2p_addressbook_subs` — one per subscribed addressbook

So the count is driven by remote peers: a STREAM ACCEPT destination invites any number of inbound streams, and each one costs a socket and a window pair before a byte of payload moves.

## What to decide

- **A cap, and a key.** `max_stream_connections`, same shape as the other three, read per admission so a zero still works without a restart.
- **Whether it shares SAM's admission instance or gets its own.** SAM sessions and stream connections are different resources — a session is a handshake budget, a stream conn is sockets and buffers — and #41D5PFF's argument for one instance per resource applies. But they are both client-facing, so this is a judgement call rather than a lookup.
- **What a refusal does.** `m:i2p_sam_session` gets `{error, _}` back from a refused session today and closes the socket; a refused stream conn needs the same answer at every one of the three call sites, and the STREAM ACCEPT path has a client waiting on a SAM reply.
- **A counter**, in the same section as #41D5PFF's three: at the cap this fires on every inbound stream, so a rate an operator watches, and today a cap-less resource has nothing to report at all.

add.issue.name: The SAM listener's three control functions have no bound on their wait

edit.description.md:
Found while doing #EP6SRK1, and deliberately left out of it: that ticket was a rate limit and this is a wait.

## The gap

`m:i2p_sam_listener`'s three control functions have a `receive` with **no timeout clause**:

```erlang
port(Listener) -> ... receive {port, Ref, P} -> P end.
address(Listener) -> ... receive {address, Ref, Address} -> Address end.
stop(Listener) -> ... receive {stopped, Ref} -> ok end.
```

So a caller of any of them waits forever if the listener is gone, wedged, or exiting. `m:i2p_ntcp2_listener:port/1` and `address/1` bound theirs at `?CONTROL_TIMEOUT_MS` (1000) and raise `{listener_unanswered, Listener, Question}`; `m:i2p_ntcp2_listener:stop/1` kills the listener and answers `ok` rather than waiting.

**#EP6SRK1 made this worse, not better, and that is the reason to file it now.** Before that ticket the listener answered a control message from its `receive` even when it was mid-poll, so a caller rarely waited on anything. After it the listener is a pure control loop with an acceptor beside it, which is the right shape -- and a control path that is blocked is now a caller with no bound at all, rather than one that waits at most a second. The behaviour that changed is narrow; the exposure was always there.

It is on the operator-facing client path: `m:i2per_status` and any other presentation app calls into a router's exported state, and a supervisor restart of the SAM listener is an ordinary event.

## Do

- [ ] `port/1` and `address/1` bound their waits and raise `m:i2p_ntcp2_listener`'s `{listener_unanswered, _, _}` shape, so the two listeners answer the same question the same way.
- [ ] `stop/1` answers `ok` whether or not the listener was alive to be asked, by monitoring and killing -- the acceptor's blocked `f:gen_tcp:accept/1` ends on the socket closing, so a kill is a sufficient stop.
- [ ] **Whether the reply shapes are unified at the same time.** They are not interchangeable today: this module answers `{stopped, Ref}` and `m:i2p_ntcp2_listener` answers `{stop, Ref, stopped}`. #EP6SRK1 introduced a third answer by copying the NTCP2 line into this module and breaking `stop/1` for two days, which the suite caught immediately. One shape, or a comment at both ends saying they differ and why.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Solution: the accept loop moved to a process of its own, and the NTCP2 one generalised to share it

### The decision the ticket asked for: one acceptor, not two

**`m:i2p_ntcp2_acceptor` is now `m:i2p_tcp_acceptor`, and SAM uses it.** The ticket framed this as "reuse or write a SAM one"; the answer is neither, because what is duplicated is not the transport logic.

The loop is `accept`, set options, call a handler, recurse. The *policy* -- what an accepted socket becomes -- is a `f:handler/1` the listener builds once and passes in the start arguments, so it crosses the process boundary **once, at start**, not per connection; the per-connection cost is a local fun call. The split that leaves: **the acceptor owns the accept and the socket, the listener owns what the socket becomes.** The NTCP2 responder spec and the SAM session spec each stay in their own module, next to the announcement the new owner owes.

A second acceptor would have cost a second copy of the loop, and the copy is exactly where two would have drifted. It already had: the two listeners answer `{stop, Ref, stopped}` and `{stopped, Ref}` for the same question (below), and I copied the wrong one.

What made me decide rather than default: the old acceptor's doc is **entirely general** -- the driver detail, the active-mode inheritance, the handover window, the lifetime. Only the `role => bob` child spec was NTCP2's. Generalising the module made that doc better rather than worse, and the two handover comments now each say what their own resource adds.

### Demonstrated red

Restoring the pre-split shape -- the listener accepting alone on a **one-second** `after`, no acceptor at all -- and running the new case with 6 connections and a 2000 ms budget:

```
a_batch_of_inbound_sessions_is_not_accepted_one_per_second: FAILED
  {accept_batch_incomplete, 1}
```

One session inside the budget, not four and not six: the first tick accepts one and five are still waiting when the budget expires. The defect's floor for N=6 is (N-1) = 5 s against a 2 s bound, so the bound is under half of what the defect needed rather than a tolerance that happens to clear it.

**A first attempt at that demonstration passed, and why is worth recording.** I restored the one-second poll but left the acceptor running beside it, so the acceptor was still accepting at full speed and the case had nothing to prove. A second attempt reported `{badmatch,{asked,{127,0,0,1}}}` -- also not the defect, but my patch had not applied cleanly and shifted the arguments of `control_loop/4`, so `port/1` answered with the address. Neither was a green case; both were the wrong red, which is worth as little as a green for the wrong reason.

Continues below.

add.issue.comment.md:
### Two bugs of my own, both caught by the suite within the hour

**The reply shape.** I wrote `From ! {stop, Ref, stopped}` into `m:i2p_sam_listener` -- the NTCP2 shape -- while its own `stop/1` matches `{stopped, Ref}`. `sam_listener_binds_loopback` hung to the timetrap. The two listeners multiplex control messages differently and the shapes are not interchangeable. There is now a comment at the send saying exactly that, and #YJ0DSAT asks whether they should be unified rather than left to be re-mixed.

**The handler contract.** `m:i2p_tcp_acceptor` asserts `ok = Handler(Sock)`, and it earned its place on first use. `m:i2p_sam_listener:handover/2` ended in a send, and `erlang:send/2` returns *its first argument*, so the handler was answering `{socket_ready, Sock}`. My first fix made it worse: `ok = SessionPid ! {socket_ready, Sock}` can never match, because the send returns the message. The correct form is an explicit `ok` as the last expression, and the acceptor's doc now names both traps and says why the assertion is the pin rather than noise.

### Item four: the handover invariant, stated where it is load-bearing

`m:i2p_sam_listener:handover/2` now carries the ordering and why it cannot be done any other way. The part worth having: `m:i2p_sam_session:init/1` *cannot* activate the socket itself, because a process that does not own a socket cannot set options on it and would fail before the handover had run. So the socket travels in the child spec and the go-ahead arrives as a message -- `controlling_process/2` first, then `{socket_ready, Sock}`, and the session's `{active, once}` is the first moment a peer byte can be delivered.

The acceptor also now sets `{active, false}` on the accepted socket rather than relying on the listen socket's option, so the invariant does not rest on a caller's `f:gen_tcp:listen/1`.

### Gate

erlfmt clean, dialyzer clean (exit 0), **951 eunit** (unchanged), **224 CT** (+1), `just doc` builds. Re-run on the final tree.

### Not in this ticket

**`m:i2p_sam_sup:start_stream_conn/1` is untouched** and still ungated -- #GS6VKZ8, filed earlier this session.

**`port/1`, `address/1` and `stop/1` still have no bound on their wait.** This ticket did not create that, but it removed the one thing that made it rare: the listener no longer answers a control message from inside a poll, so a blocked control path is now a caller with no bound rather than one that waits a second. Filed as #YJ0DSAT, tagged `from-review`, with the NTCP2 answers it should adopt.

add.issue.name: The dial path throws away the SSU2 failure reason, so a park is invisible

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Todo (0.2.0).** Filed in Backlog because the board's Todo lane is currently unresolvable for writes -- see the lane defect noted on #HXT1P2D.

## What to build

Make the outbound dial report **why** it abandoned a transport. Today the reason is discarded in one line, so a dial parked on a dead transport is indistinguishable from one that is merely early.

## The discard

~~~erlang
%% i2p_peer.erl:996
{error, _Reason} ->
    fallback
~~~

`await_ssu2_connection/2` already carries the session's exit reason out as `{error, Info}` all the way here. Nothing downstream can tell a dead port from a protocol error from a timeout.

## What the reason already distinguishes

| exit | source | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{handshake_timeout, session_request}` | `i2p_ssu2_conn.erl:573` | we sent, **nothing came back** |
| `{protocol_error, session_request}` | `:506` | **something came back** and was wrong |
| `{protocol_error, created_decode}` | `:827` | ditto |
| `{protocol_error, router_info}` | `:850` | ditto |
| `{protocol_error, static_key_mismatch}` | `:859` | ditto |
| `{relay_rejected, Code}` | `:1467` | introducer path: the introducer refused |
| `{relay_bad_response_sig, Nonce}` | `:1469` | introducer path: signature failed |
| `{session_admission_failed, Reason}` | `:1514` | introducer path: admission refused |

**A protocol error is proof that UDP works in that direction.** A timeout is silence. That is the whole discriminator, and it is currently thrown away.

## Why this matters more than it looks

`CONTEXT.md` already has this pattern for reachability: reported with a separate **reason**, naming where the chain broke, because *the reasons exist because the distinction is what makes a failure diagnosable*. The dial path is the one surface where it is missing.

Per dial, a timeout cannot separate *our UDP is blocked* from *that peer is down*. **Across peers it can**: SSU2 timing out for every peer while NTCP2 succeeds for every peer means the common cause is ours -- and that is the actionable one, because "your UDP is blocked" is an operator-fixable configuration fact while "peer X is UDP-dead" is not actionable at all.

Neither reference implementation can do this. i2p-java carries an open TODO admitting it cannot detect "UDP is completely blocked"; i2pd does not attempt it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The SSU2 failure reason survives to wherever it is reported. No `_Reason` on this path.
- [ ] A counter for parks, distinguishable from `peer_connect_failed`, which only fires once **both** legs have failed.
- [ ] An event carrying the reason, so `{protocol_error, _}` and `{handshake_timeout, _}` are separately visible.
- [ ] A test asserts the two reasons are distinguished -- not that a fallback happens.

add.issue.name: The read API reports a peer parked mid-SSU2 as ntcp2, and flattens `connecting` into `other`

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Todo (0.2.0).** Filed in Backlog because the board's Todo lane is currently unresolvable for writes -- see the lane defect noted on #HXT1P2D.

## What to build

Two present-tense lies in a contract the map froze as public. Both fixes are additive.

## Lie one: `transport` reports the creation-time default, not the attempt

~~~erlang
%% i2p_peer.erl:889 -- set when the peer entry is CREATED, before any decision
transport => ntcp2,

%% i2p_peer.erl:369 -- and read back with that same value as its fallback
transport => maps:get(transport, PeerState, ntcp2)
~~~

A peer parked in an SSU2 attempt -- up to 10 s direct, up to 60 s through an introducer -- reports `transport => ntcp2`. Actively misleading, not merely absent.

## Lie two: `connecting` is indistinguishable from `backoff`

~~~erlang
%% i2p_status_data.erl:151-162
    (#{status := connected}, Acc) -> ...;
    (_, Acc) -> maps:update_with(other, fun(N) -> N + 1 end, 1, Acc)
~~~

`connecting`, `backoff` and `none` all land in `other`. An operator cannot tell a dial in flight from a peer being retried from one we have given up on.

## Also missing

`i2p_peer:status/0` exposes `status`, `attempts` and `transport` -- but **not `last_attempt`**, the one field whose age reveals a park. And `attempts` stays 0 while a dial is parked, so `connecting` at `attempts = 0` is exactly what a healthy dial looks like 5 ms in.

## Why additive is safe

`CONTEXT.md`: the status view "is a public contract: consumers other than the core depend on it, so its shape changes only additively within a version." A corrected `transport` value and a new `connecting` bucket are both additive.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `transport` reports the transport actually being attempted, not the creation-time default.
- [ ] `connecting` is distinguishable from `backoff` in the aggregated view.
- [ ] `last_attempt` is exposed, so a parked dial is distinguishable from a fresh one.
- [ ] A test asserts a peer mid-SSU2-attempt does not report `ntcp2`.

From #HXT1P2D. Scratchpad `01M3Z41FMVCD32JTAR7AK0TNYX`.

add.issue.name: Transport setting becomes three values: no udp / enable udp / prefer udp

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Todo (0.2.0).** Filed in Backlog because the board's Todo lane is currently unresolvable for writes -- see the lane defect noted on #HXT1P2D.

## What to build

Replace the boolean `ssu2_enabled` with three values, because the boolean welds two unrelated properties together.

## The conflation

`ssu2_enabled = false` was never "do not dial over UDP". It does three things:

| call site | effect of `false` |
|---|---|
| `i2per_sup.erl:363` | no SSU2 listener bound at boot |
| `i2p_identity.erl:133` | **no SSU2 address published in our RouterInfo** |
| `i2p_peer.erl:932`, `:1624` | SSU2 not tried when dialing |

So an operator who wants to serve UDP but reach for TCP first cannot say so -- they must also give up inbound UDP reachability, which is a change to **network credibility**, not a local preference.

## The three values

| | serve UDP (listener + published address) | reach for UDP first |
|---|---|---|
| `no udp` | no | no |
| `enable udp` | **yes** | **no** |
| `prefer udp` | yes | yes |

`enable udp` is the state that is unrepresentable today. It is not invented: i2p-java's bid values land on it -- SSU2 65 vs NTCP2 70 unestablished (a 5 ms spread, effectively a tie), then **NTCP2 25 vs SSU2 50 established**. Java serves both and prefers TCP once it has a session.

An enum also forbids the incoherent fourth combination (serve=no, dial=yes) by construction, which two independent booleans would not.

## Surface

**Config file only, boot-time. No control in the presentation app** -- i2pd works this way, and a runtime flip is filed separately.

Backwards-compatible in *meaning*: today's `true` becomes `prefer udp`, today's `false` becomes `no udp`. Nothing silently changes what it means.

## Also needed

- `config/sys.config` has **no `ssu2_enabled` line today**; the only mention outside source is one line in `docs/protocol.md`, which is a protocol document and not an operator guide. Ship a commented default and an operator-facing entry.
- The operator-facing entry must say **the choice is permanent until restart**. There is no runtime escape, and an operator who sets `prefer udp` on a UDP-blocked network has no way back but a reboot. That hazard belongs on the logging-floor checklist (#SEW8DCM), not only in prose.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Three values, with the incoherent combination unrepresentable.
- [ ] `enable udp` serves UDP and dials TCP first.
- [ ] A commented default in `sys.config` and an operator-facing doc entry saying the choice is boot-time.
- [ ] Every existing `ssu2_enabled` call site updated, and the test suite's `arm_ssu2/1` too.

From #HXT1P2D. Scratchpad `01M3Z41FMV0VJY0FG6G9PJ55XJ`, `01M3Z41FMVCD32JTAR7AK0TNYX`. Glossary terms added to CONTEXT.md in `89d6ce11`.

add.issue.name: A dial that raises strands its peer in `connecting` for the life of the process

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Todo (0.2.0).** Filed in Backlog because the board's Todo lane is currently unresolvable for writes -- see the lane defect noted on #HXT1P2D.

## What to build

Supervision for the outbound dial, so a dial that **raises** rather than returns cannot leave a peer stuck.

## The strand

The dial is a bare unlinked spawn:

~~~erlang
%% i2p_peer.erl:884 and :905
spawn(fun() -> init_connect(PeerHash, ...) end)
~~~

No link, no monitor. And `connecting` has no way out:

- `maybe_connect_status(connecting, _PeerHash, State) -> State` (`:897`) -- no timer, no re-dial.
- `idle_peer/1` (`:590-593`) refuses to evict a `connecting` peer, **deliberately** (`:553-558`: evicting would let the dial complete into a `peers` entry that is gone, and `handle_conn_started/4` answers `error` for an unknown peer by stopping the connection -- so the dial would be torn down by its own successful handshake).

So if `init_connect/3` raises, there is no `{connect_failed, ...}`, no `DOWN`, and `enter_backoff/2` is never reached. The peer sits at `status => connecting` for the life of the router process, with `attempts` at 0 and `last_attempt` frozen at the spawn instant.

## Raise sites on that path

- `true = is_pid(Manager)` -- `i2p_peer.erl:985`, `:1057`
- `case dialable_remote_opts(BobOpts) of {ok, DialBobOpts} ->` -- `:1036`, **no `error` clause**, so a `case_clause` is one `pick_introducer/3` change away
- anything `i2p_ssu2_conn:connect/4` raises rather than returns

## Why this is its own ticket

The fix is `spawn_monitor` plus a deadline on `connecting` -- a supervision decision. #HXT1P2D settled it belongs on its own so neither change hides behind the other.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A dial process that exits abnormally produces a terminal message, so `connecting` is always escapable.
- [ ] `connecting` has a deadline, or cannot persist indefinitely.
- [ ] The deliberate "never evict a `connecting` peer" rule is preserved -- it is right, and the fix must not break the case it exists for.
- [ ] A test crashes a dial process and asserts the peer does not stay `connecting`.

From #HXT1P2D.

add.issue.name: Bound the three dial parks: one derived number each, and redesign the fallback test

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Backlog.** Every park here only exists for operators who have opted into SSU2 -- `ssu2_enabled()` defaults to false, so i2per ships NTCP2-only. It is bounded latency on an opt-in path.

## What to build

Three inline literals currently bound an outbound dial, and none of them is derived from the thing it is bounding.

| literal | what it actually is |
|---|---|
| `?RETRY_MS` x `?MAX_RESENDS`, 1 Hz x 9, ~10 s (`i2p_ssu2_conn.erl:60,68`) | a **deliberate divergence** from the spec's 1.25/2.5/5 s / 15 s schedule: send more, give up sooner. Keep. |
| `await_ssu2_connection(Pid, 20000)` (`:239`, `:241`) | almost certainly the spec's **20 s whole-handshake** figure applied to the wrong phase. A correct ceiling for the wrong thing, and dead in practice because the eager retransmit budget wins the race. |
| `await_ssu2_redirect(Pid, 60000)` (`:304`, `:306`) | **attached to the wrong quantity.** See below. |

## Why 60000 is wrong

The SSU2 spec's entire normative statement on the introducer relay token is one sentence with no number: "The token must be used immediately by Alice in the Session Request" (ssu2.md:2450). There is no `expires` field on the RelayResponse block; the published `iexp` bounds publication, not a dial attempt. **The number is chosen, not derived.**

`git blame` puts the line in the root commit `f694ecc [RELEASE-0.1.0] Initial public release` with no commit message, and i2p-java has `RELAY_TOKEN_LIFETIME = 60*1000L` -- exactly 60000 -- bounding *Charlie's token acceptance window*, a different quantity, where in Java it never binds because `MAX_OB_ESTABLISH_TIME = 25 s` is shorter. Strong evidence the constant was ported and attached to the wrong thing; provenance unconfirmable.

The two reference implementations disagree by 5x on this path: i2pd **5 s**, armed as its first action before connecting to Bob so one timer spans the whole path; i2p-java **25 s** for the whole path and `OB_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT = 15 s` for the relay phase specifically.

## Decision

**15 s** for the introducer path. It sits between the two implementations rather than picking a side, and it makes the eager retransmit budget rather than the outer literal the thing that fires first -- which is what already happens on the direct leg.

## One number per park

Each outer literal should be derived from the session's own budget so the two cannot disagree -- which is precisely why 20000 never fires.

## The test, redesigned

`transport_falls_back_to_ntcp2` currently costs ~11 s and asserts nothing about the product: it asserts a fallback happened inside a 60 s timetrap. **If the product's bound were 59 seconds it would pass.**

The 11 s is not the 20000 literal -- it is the eager retransmit budget, and that budget is **already an app-env lever** (`handshake_retry_ms`, `handshake_max_resends`). This suite already has the pattern for exactly this, and states the rule in `arm_sndbuf/1`'s comment: *"the case reaches the stall through a production lever rather than a private mechanism."*

- add `arm_handshake_budget/1` setting `handshake_retry_ms` to 50 and `handshake_max_resends` to 2 -- park becomes ~150 ms
- unset both in `end_per_testcase/2`
- timetrap back to 30 s with every other case
- tighten the inner bounds to a multiple of the configured park
- **keep the CT timetrap**: it asserts nothing about the product, it is the harness's liveness guarantee, and `i2p_admission:admit/2` is a real `gen_server:call(..., infinity)` on this path
- upgrade the assertion from "a fallback happened within 60 s" to the **policy**: SSU2 attempted and abandoned, NTCP2 second, ended on NTCP2

This makes the test stronger, not weaker: configured, it can tell a correct bound from a reintroduced hardcoded literal, which today it cannot tell at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Three parks, three numbers, each derived from the session's own budget.
- [ ] The introducer path's bound is 15 s, and the reason it is chosen rather than derived is written down.
- [ ] The fallback test completes in well under a second and asserts the policy, not a timetrap.
- [ ] `transport_falls_back_to_ntcp2` keeps its 60 s timetrap replaced by the suite default, and the CT timetrap is still in force.

From #HXT1P2D. Scratchpad `01M3Z41FMVG4ZKHZWD5WNE2YVP`.

add.issue.name: Hot-flip the dial transport preference without a restart

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Backlog. Explicitly post-1.0.0** -- by the map's own definition 1.0.0 is "a full match to i2pd as it is today", and i2pd cannot flip transport preference at runtime, so a hot flip is *beyond* parity rather than parity work. (Maintainer: "It is ok that is how i2pd works.")

## What to build

Change the transport preference without restarting the router, so an operator who discovers their UDP is blocked can say so rather than waiting for a reboot.

## Why it is cheap for the dial half and expensive for the publish half

- The **dial preference** is one `andalso` at `i2p_peer.erl:932` (and `:1624` in `dialable_ri/1`). Making that hot is small.
- The **availability** half is `i2per_sup.erl:363` (supervision tree) plus `i2p_identity.erl:133` (our own signed RouterInfo, republished to the network). Not hot material.

**Only the dial preference is in scope.** A hot availability flip is a separate and much larger piece of work.

## The hazard this closes

The three-way setting is boot-time and config-file-only, so a wrong choice is wrong **for the life of the process**. An operator who sets `prefer udp` on a UDP-blocked network currently has no way back but a reboot, and the only evidence they will get is the counter showing NTCP2 succeeding while SSU2 times out -- long after the decision.

That makes the counters from the sibling instrument tickets load-bearing rather than decorative: they are the only evidence an operator will ever get that their boot-time preference is contradicted. `CONTEXT.md` already has the vocabulary -- an operator's assertion is **configured** reachability, and what would contradict it is **measured**.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The dial preference can change at runtime without disturbing in-flight dials or established connections.
- [ ] The change is observable -- logged, and visible in the status view.
- [ ] The boot-time availability half is explicitly out of scope and stays boot-only.

From #HXT1P2D.

add.issue.name: SSU2 congestion control and RTT estimation

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

**Intended lane: Backlog. Not to move to Todo until after 1.0.0** (maintainer's call, #HXT1P2D).

> **Scope conflict to resolve:** the map's *Not yet specified* places congestion control in **0.3.0** ("0.3.0's shape beyond the two decided tickets... Beyond them: congestion control and RTT estimation, which is where the byte counters from 0.2.0 finally get a consumer"). This decision places it after **1.0.0**. The map needs correcting to whichever is right.

## What to build

i2per's SSU2 has **no congestion control and no send-side flow control**. The congestion block is carried, parsed, re-encoded, and then never acted on.

~~~erlang
%% i2p_ssu2.erl
-define(BLOCK_CONGESTION, 21).
block_data({congestion, Flags}) -> tlv(?BLOCK_CONGESTION, <<Flags:8>>).   %% :608
decode_block(?BLOCK_CONGESTION, <<Flags:8>>) -> {congestion, Flags}.       %% :764
~~~

There is no `cwnd`, no `ssthresh`, no send window and no rate limit anywhere in `apps/i2per/src`.

The only window in the SSU2 path is the **receive** window -- the ACK range reach from #7GP4A4K -- which bounds what we accept, not what we send. So backpressure is the peer's receive window, and congestion is discovered by losing packets.

NTCP2 sits on a `gen_tcp` socket and inherits the kernel's congestion control and flow control. That is the actual trade for TCP's per-packet overhead and head-of-line blocking.

## Consequence

SSU2's per-packet cheapness is real, but in i2per specifically it is offset by having no CC. **Preferring SSU2 for a sustained loaded session means preferring the transport i2per implements worst.**

This matches i2p-java's bid structure arrived at independently: SSU2 65 vs NTCP2 70 unestablished (effectively a tie), then **NTCP2 25 vs SSU2 50 established**. Java prefers TCP once it has a session.

So "UDP is more efficient" is not yet a reason for i2per to prefer it for load -- and that is why the dial policy settled on preferring the transport that is known-good rather than the one that is theoretically cheaper.

## RTT estimation

The same gap. It is what a transport-preference *delay* would have needed to be meaningful: any stagger short enough to rescue a dead port fires before a healthy introducer dial finishes (~4.5 RTTs against ~1 RTT for a direct dial), and with no RTT estimate there is no way to make the constant relative. The reference implementations are in the same position.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] SSU2 send rate is governed by something, not left to the peer's receive window.
- [ ] The congestion block the peer already sends is acted on, or the omission is documented as a divergence.
- [ ] RTT is estimated and exposed, so any future transport delay can be expressed relative to it.

From #HXT1P2D. Scratchpad `01M3Z41FMVWSQYM0W9R48PM0YM`.

add.issue.comment.md:
**Decision, 2026-10-02. Two tickets land in 0.2.0; five land after it.**

**The premise was wrong three ways.**

1. The 20 s is a ceiling, not the cost. On a dead UDP port the session's own retransmit budget fires first (`?RETRY_MS` x `?MAX_RESENDS` = 1 Hz x 9, ~10 s) -- which is why the test times at 11 s. The `20000` is reached only when SessionCreated arrives and SessionConfirmed is then lost.
2. There is a third park, three times worse, undocumented: `await_ssu2_redirect(Pid, 60000)` at `i2p_ssu2_conn.erl:304`, the firewalled-remote path. **A peer publishing firewalled SSU2 *plus* published NTCP2 costs up to 60 s before TCP is tried** -- exactly the "reachable on only one" case the ticket asks about.
3. The compounding argument is stale: the dial is a bare `spawn/1` (`i2p_peer.erl:884`), so dials are concurrent, and ZYQ227K is fixed (`e14b5177`).

**And the blast radius is smaller than filed.** `ssu2_enabled()` defaults to **false** (`i2p_identity.erl:319`) -- i2per ships NTCP2-only. Every park exists only for operators who opted in.

**Decided**

- **All three parks are one decision**, and where a spec exists it is tested against. The direct leg is spec-anchored (Session Request 1.25/2.5/5 s, 15 s establishment, 20 s whole handshake). The introducer leg is **silent**: the spec's entire normative statement is "the token must be used immediately", no number, no field to carry one.
- **Introducer park: 15 s** (#SV6S264). Chosen, not derived. i2pd uses 5 s; i2p-java 25 s for the path, 15 s for the relay phase. 60 s is looser than both -- and `git blame` puts it in the root commit with no message, while i2p-java has `RELAY_TOKEN_LIFETIME = 60*1000L` bounding a *different* quantity, where it never binds because 25 s is shorter.
- **The instrument is the precondition of the policy, not a companion.** You cannot learn "SSU2 gave up" without a fact saying so, and the reason that would tell you is discarded at `i2p_peer.erl:996`.
- **Three transport settings** -- `no udp` / `enable udp` / `prefer udp` -- config-file only, boot-time, no presentation-app control, as i2pd (#75YRPJ7). The middle state is unrepresentable today: `ssu2_enabled = false` also stops us *publishing* an SSU2 address, which is a change to network credibility, not a preference. Glossary in `89d6ce11`.
- **In `prefer udp`, hold both and keep TCP until UDP is confirmed, dropping TCP on expiry.** Boot-only means no operator escape, so the automatic fallback must land on the known-good transport. Converges on i2p-java: NTCP2 25 vs SSU2 50 once established.
- **Racing is not adopted.** It buys latency and no knowledge -- SSU2-first already teaches both branches -- and it doubles the handshake load the 0.1.0 identity forbids.

**Why a UDP-blocked peer cannot be detected per-dial.** Silence is over-determined: our UDP blocked, the peer down, a middlebox. Only a third-party observation separates them -- the peer test, 0.3.0 material, which is why i2p-java carries an open TODO admitting the same. **But the discriminator exists and is thrown away:** `{handshake_timeout, _}` means nothing came back; `{protocol_error, _}` means something did and was wrong, proof UDP works that way. Across peers that aggregates into "our UDP is blocked" -- the actionable one.

**The test.** The 11 s is not the 20000 literal -- it is the retransmit budget, which is *already an app-env lever*. `arm_sndbuf/1` states the rule three functions above: reach the stall "through a production lever rather than a private mechanism". Arming it small takes the fallback case to ~150 ms and lets it assert the **policy** rather than a 60 s timetrap about itself. The CT timetrap stays: it is the harness's liveness guarantee, not an assertion, and `i2p_admission:admit/2` is a real `gen_server:call(..., infinity)` on this path.

**Filed:** 0.2.0 -- #1Q4JREN, #X7BP9G1, #75YRPJ7, #8V1Z06A. Backlog -- #SV6S264, #0JJ375C, #RC68AGE (last two post-1.0.0).

add.issue.comment.author: TP6W3VE8AVTJX96RZ4R7RNZVCX

edit.description.md:
## Destination

**i2per 0.2.0: a release an operator who did not write it can run, and see.**

Two claims, and the point of this release is that **both are checkable using the things 0.2.0 itself ships**:

1. *We ship a versioned, public read API over the router's state.* Cumulative byte counters at the transport boundary **and** the transit relay, uptime, tunnel-build outcomes, and a documented additive-only contract, with `i2p_stats` as the counter home inside the core. The core supplies data; a presentation app aggregates.
2. *We ship a logging floor.* All eight standard levels with a written discipline, `notice` as the default, a hot `log_level` key, a configurable formatter, and a 3am checklist of what must be recorded for a fault to be diagnosable without reading the source.

Plus the boundaries that keep both sustainable: the core is data-only and never renders ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-data-only-core-with-presentation-apps.md)), and deployment is a separate repository.

**What 0.2.0 deliberately does not do: change network behaviour.**

Being a Charlie and measuring reachability — the two claims this map originally targeted — move to **0.3.0**. The reasoning is verification, not size. Those are protocol claims, and their only oracle is the i2pd interop suite, which does not run in CI. Telemetry and logging let you *debug* a protocol claim; they cannot *verify* it. So the two groups have different verification stories, and the observability release is the one whose claims are self-verifying. Building it first is what makes 0.3.0 provable rather than merely done.

The decisions on those two tickets already stand and are not reopened by this re-draw. Only their release assignment moves.
## Notes

**Domain:** an Erlang/OTP I2P router (`apps/i2per`) plus a standalone status web service (`apps/i2per_status`). `i2per` is the model provider, not a person.

**Vocabulary** — the I2P spec's, not i2pd's. This map pins down three terms the tree currently uses loosely:

- **Charlie** — the router an *Alice* asks to introduce it to a *Bob*. i2per is currently an Alice only. "Being a Charlie" is the 0.2.0 claim.
- **Measured reachability** — reachability established by an actual peer test, as opposed to the current config echo.
- **Network credibility** — how the live network treats i2per: whether peers can intros it, and whether it can intros them.
- **Core** — the `i2per` application itself: transports, tunnels, NetDb, SAM. It exposes state through Erlang APIs only, and **never** has a GUI or TUI and never serves HTTP.
- **Presentation app** — a separate OTP application that connects to a core node over Erlang distribution and supplies a GUI, TUI, or external API for others to consume. `i2per_status` is the first. Both same-node and separate-node operation are supported.

**Release roadmap** (maintainer's): **0.1.0 is not finished yet** — the repo's 0.1.0 is still a development snapshot, not a published release. **0.2.0** is the destination of this map. **1.0.0 is a full match to i2pd as it is today**, still excluding the legacy protocols. So the i2pd-parity items — tunnel build v2, Charlie selection, congestion control and RTT, hole-punch Half B, LeaseSet v1, SOCKS/HTTP proxy/BOB/I2PControl, TUN, console CLI — are 1.0.0 material, and the map's two scope tickets should resolve that way rather than by re-litigating it.

**Owned elsewhere, deliberately not ticketed here.** 0.1.0's identity is "we can connect to the I2P network without causing harm", and the maintainer has folded making that claim explicit and tested into **finishing 0.1.0 directly**. It is not on this board and should not be re-filed here. Worth knowing why it is not a trivial claim: the property already holds (the shipped profile bounds transit and disables live participation, and `i2per_sup:validate_host/1` refuses a non-public published host unless `allow_private_host` is set), but nothing tests it — which means a future change could quietly break the one property the release is named for.

**Standing preferences:**

- **A test that can flake is a design or test defect, not bad luck.** The
  maintainer's rule, added 2026-09-28 after three flakes in one session were
  investigated: in Erlang a test can be made deterministic, so a non-deterministic
  test means something has not been synchronised on. The distinctions that matter:
  a **barrier** is a received message, a monitor, or a `gen_server:call` issued
  after the event — all of which are ordered by the runtime and cannot race; a
  **deadline** is a hope, and a **tolerance** is a flake with extra steps that has
  also given up the ability to fail. Polling a state predicate until a deadline is
  a barrier in disguise and is treated as one. So is a `timer:sleep` whose
  guarantee is asserted (`Uptime >= 1500` after sleeping 1500) — that cannot fail
  on a fast machine, unlike a sleep that hopes some work has finished. A property
  that cannot be tested without moving the system clock, or a hostile scheduler,
  is documented as untested rather than covered by a case that re-asserts
  something adjacent under a misleading name.

## What to build

i2per's SSU2 has **no congestion control and no send-side flow control**. The congestion block is carried, parsed, re-encoded, and then never acted on.

~~~erlang
%% i2p_ssu2.erl
-define(BLOCK_CONGESTION, 21).
block_data({congestion, Flags}) -> tlv(?BLOCK_CONGESTION, <<Flags:8>>).   %% :608
decode_block(?BLOCK_CONGESTION, <<Flags:8>>) -> {congestion, Flags}.       %% :764
~~~

There is no `cwnd`, no `ssthresh`, no send window and no rate limit anywhere in `apps/i2per/src`.

The only window in the SSU2 path is the **receive** window -- the ACK range reach from #7GP4A4K -- which bounds what we accept, not what we send. So backpressure is the peer's receive window, and congestion is discovered by losing packets.

NTCP2 sits on a `gen_tcp` socket and inherits the kernel's congestion control and flow control. That is the actual trade for TCP's per-packet overhead and head-of-line blocking.

## Consequence

SSU2's per-packet cheapness is real, but in i2per specifically it is offset by having no CC. **Preferring SSU2 for a sustained loaded session means preferring the transport i2per implements worst.**

This matches i2p-java's bid structure arrived at independently: SSU2 65 vs NTCP2 70 unestablished (effectively a tie), then **NTCP2 25 vs SSU2 50 established**. Java prefers TCP once it has a session.

So "UDP is more efficient" is not yet a reason for i2per to prefer it for load -- and that is why the dial policy settled on preferring the transport that is known-good rather than the one that is theoretically cheaper.

## RTT estimation

The same gap. It is what a transport-preference *delay* would have needed to be meaningful: any stagger short enough to rescue a dead port fires before a healthy introducer dial finishes (~4.5 RTTs against ~1 RTT for a direct dial), and with no RTT estimate there is no way to make the constant relative. The reference implementations are in the same position.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] SSU2 send rate is governed by something, not left to the peer's receive window.
- [ ] The congestion block the peer already sends is acted on, or the omission is documented as a divergence.
- [ ] RTT is estimated and exposed, so any future transport delay can be expressed relative to it.

## The premise does not hold: the per-case cost is ~5 ms, not ~1.9 s

Criterion 1 asked for the per-case cost to be attributed before anything changed. I measured it. It is **4.7-5.5 ms**, and the ~420 s the ticket attributes to per-testcase lifecycle is **not in the per-testcase lifecycle** — it is second-resolution rounding in `suite.log`, plus two broken cases in one suite.

### What was measured, and how

Three measurements, each timed with `erlang:monotonic_time/1` rather than read off a log:

**1. Component costs in isolation** (25 rounds, one untimed warm-up first — the first `ensure_all_started` in a fresh node pays module loading for the whole tree and would otherwise be attributed to every case):

| component | mean | median | p95 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ensure_all_started` + `application:stop` | 1.34-1.67 ms | 1.34-1.63 ms | 1.5-2.7 ms |
| SSU2 trace handler add + remove | 0.05-0.21 ms | 0.04-0.09 ms | 0.07-0.47 ms |

edit.description.md:
## Destination

**i2per 0.2.0: a release an operator who did not write it can run, and see.**

Two claims, and the point of this release is that **both are checkable using the things 0.2.0 itself ships**:

1. *We ship a versioned, public read API over the router's state.* Cumulative byte counters at the transport boundary **and** the transit relay, uptime, tunnel-build outcomes, and a documented additive-only contract, with `i2p_stats` as the counter home inside the core. The core supplies data; a presentation app aggregates.
2. *We ship a logging floor.* All eight standard levels with a written discipline, `notice` as the default, a hot `log_level` key, a configurable formatter, and a 3am checklist of what must be recorded for a fault to be diagnosable without reading the source.

Plus the boundaries that keep both sustainable: the core is data-only and never renders ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-data-only-core-with-presentation-apps.md)), and deployment is a separate repository.

**What 0.2.0 deliberately does not do: change network behaviour.**

Being a Charlie and measuring reachability — the two claims this map originally targeted — move to **0.3.0**. The reasoning is verification, not size. Those are protocol claims, and their only oracle is the i2pd interop suite, which does not run in CI. Telemetry and logging let you *debug* a protocol claim; they cannot *verify* it. So the two groups have different verification stories, and the observability release is the one whose claims are self-verifying. Building it first is what makes 0.3.0 provable rather than merely done.

The decisions on those two tickets already stand and are not reopened by this re-draw. Only their release assignment moves.
## Notes

**Domain:** an Erlang/OTP I2P router (`apps/i2per`) plus a standalone status web service (`apps/i2per_status`). `i2per` is the model provider, not a person.

**Vocabulary** — the I2P spec's, not i2pd's. This map pins down three terms the tree currently uses loosely:

- **Charlie** — the router an *Alice* asks to introduce it to a *Bob*. i2per is currently an Alice only. "Being a Charlie" is the 0.2.0 claim.
- **Measured reachability** — reachability established by an actual peer test, as opposed to the current config echo.
- **Network credibility** — how the live network treats i2per: whether peers can intros it, and whether it can intros them.
- **Core** — the `i2per` application itself: transports, tunnels, NetDb, SAM. It exposes state through Erlang APIs only, and **never** has a GUI or TUI and never serves HTTP.
- **Presentation app** — a separate OTP application that connects to a core node over Erlang distribution and supplies a GUI, TUI, or external API for others to consume. `i2per_status` is the first. Both same-node and separate-node operation are supported.

**Release roadmap** (maintainer's): **0.1.0 is not finished yet** — the repo's 0.1.0 is still a development snapshot, not a published release. **0.2.0** is the destination of this map. **1.0.0 is a full match to i2pd as it is today**, still excluding the legacy protocols. So the i2pd-parity items — tunnel build v2, Charlie selection, congestion control and RTT, hole-punch Half B, LeaseSet v1, SOCKS/HTTP proxy/BOB/I2PControl, TUN, console CLI — are 1.0.0 material, and the map's two scope tickets should resolve that way rather than by re-litigating it.

**Owned elsewhere, deliberately not ticketed here.** 0.1.0's identity is "we can connect to the I2P network without causing harm", and the maintainer has folded making that claim explicit and tested into **finishing 0.1.0 directly**. It is not on this board and should not be re-filed here. Worth knowing why it is not a trivial claim: the property already holds (the shipped profile bounds transit and disables live participation, and `i2per_sup:validate_host/1` refuses a non-public published host unless `allow_private_host` is set), but nothing tests it — which means a future change could quietly break the one property the release is named for.

**Standing preferences:**

- **A test that can flake is a design or test defect, not bad luck.** The
  maintainer's rule, added 2026-09-28 after three flakes in one session were
  investigated: in Erlang a test can be made deterministic, so a non-deterministic
  test means something has not been synchronised on. The distinctions that matter:
  a **barrier** is a received message, a monitor, or a `gen_server:call` issued
  after the event — all of which are ordered by the runtime and cannot race; a
  **deadline** is a hope, and a **tolerance** is a flake with extra steps that has
  also given up the ability to fail. Polling a state predicate until a deadline is
  a barrier in disguise and is treated as one. So is a `timer:sleep` whose
  guarantee is asserted (`Uptime >= 1500` after sleeping 1500) — that cannot fail
  on a fast machine, unlike a sleep that hopes some work has finished. A property
  that cannot be tested without moving the system clock, or a hostile scheduler,
  is documented as untested rather than covered by a case that re-asserts
  something adjacent under a misleading name.
- **Data should never be duplicated.** If two places must agree about a value, one of them is the source and the other refers to it — never two hand-maintained copies. This is why the read API's key set is a single exported list, and it generalises to any contract a consumer depends on.


- **Legacy is out**, by the maintainer's call: NTCP1, SSU1, I2CP, ElGamal/DSA, Datagram1. The release profile already refuses them.
- **Instrumentation lands with the behaviour.** A ticket that touches a path adds its counters and events there. Nothing is deferred to a later ticket.
- **Gates:** `rebar.config` compiles with `warnings_as_errors`. `just check` and `just dialyzer` are release gates. The i2pd interop suite is *not* currently in `ct_opts`.
- **Both statuses are allowed:** `i2per_status` may run on the router's own node (needs no distribution, since `router_node` already defaults to `node()`) or on a separate node the operator connects. The map must not collapse this into one option.

- **Done means landed, not closed.** A ticket moves to Done when its work is merged, and **stays there until its milestone is reached** — then that milestone's whole set is closed together. The next milestone is **0.2.0**, so nothing closes before that release is published. Closing at the milestone rather than at the merge is what keeps Done readable as *what is in the next release*: closing on merge empties that list before anyone has seen the change in a build, and takes the ticket off the board while it is still the thing most worth looking at. **The exception is a wayfinder decision ticket**, whose deliverable is the decision itself — those close on resolution, because Decisions-so-far below indexes closed tickets and a resolved decision has nothing further to wait for.
**Every session consults:** `erlang`, `domain-modeling`, and `wayfinder`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket, enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link -->

- [The 0.2.0 telemetry contract: counters, events, uptime](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3H11881): a new `i2p_stats` gen_server in the core owns `counters` refs behind a public, versioned read API; bytes are counted at the transport boundary **and** the transit relay (six points); the core supplies cumulative data and the client aggregates, which is what keeps `i2p_stats` timer-free; four new events land on already-touched paths. Also settled here: the core never renders, and deployment is another repo.
- [What does i2pd's HTTP status monitor show, field for field?](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/1KJMFBH): i2pd's monitor is 22 main-page fields plus 10 detail pages (and **no graph page and no XMLRPC** — don't chase them). i2per already surfaces 7 and *holds* ~25 more, so most of it is accessor work — including the entire LeaseSets panel, the single biggest cheap win. Every **derived** value, by contrast, is new state: uptime, all six bandwidth rates, both tunnel-success ratios. Byte counting is the keystone, and no module in the tree counts a byte today.
- [What does the network require of a Charlie, and what breaks without it?](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/K84PJ0N): The role splits cleanly — an in-session half (verify RelayIntro, answer with a signed **reject**) that alone removes the real harm and needs no new crypto, plus an optional out-of-session HolePunch datagram that is not 0.2.0's problem. Nobody selects a Charlie they lack an established *outgoing* session with, so this work sequences **after** reachability, not beside it. The gap survived 0.1.0 because the protocol has no introduction-failed signal at all.

- [Three test-suite costs, and one silent coverage gap](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/T3WH4EM): EUnit 12.94 s → 9.21 s. The status poll interval becomes `poll_ms`, documented as the window the derived rates are differenced over rather than a tuning knob; the four duplicate RSA-4096 test keygens become one shared identity per run (4096 itself is fixed — `i2p_su3` accepts nothing but a 512-byte signature); and the `ct_opts` suite list is **deleted rather than policed**, so a suite on disk cannot be forgotten and the interop suite is excluded by living outside `test/`. Also settled: the biggest cost in the gate is neither of these — ~420 s of a 545 s CT run is per-testcase application start and stop ([#WA1R7SY](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/WA1R7SY)).
- [A peer whose SSU2 address does not answer costs 20 seconds before NTCP2 is tried](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/HXT1P2D): the filed premise was wrong three ways — the 20 s is a ceiling the eager retransmit budget never reaches (**~10 s is the real cost**), there is an **undocumented 60 s third park** on the firewalled-remote path that is 3× worse and lands on exactly the "reachable on only one" case the ticket asks about, and the dial is a concurrent `spawn/1`, so nothing serialises. Smaller than filed too: `ssu2_enabled` defaults to false, so **i2per ships NTCP2-only** and every park is opt-in-only. Decided: the three parks are **one** decision, spec-anchored where a spec exists — the introducer leg is **silent**, no token expiry is specified at all, so its 15 s is chosen and argued rather than derived; **the instrument is the precondition of the policy**, not a companion, because the reason that would say "SSU2 gave up" is discarded at `i2p_peer.erl:996`; and `ssu2_enabled` becomes three settings, because **transport availability and transport preference are separate terms** and `enable udp` (serve UDP, dial TCP first) is unrepresentable today. Racing rejected — it buys latency and no knowledge. Seven tickets filed; four in 0.2.0, and the two post-1.0.0 ones are the congestion-control gap and the hot transport flip.
## Not yet specified

- **Open design decisions in the status page itself** — now that the field inventory exists, these are sharp but belong past 0.2.0's two claims: does the page report *absent* services (five of i2pd's six have no i2per feature behind them) or omit them; and does i2per gain a per-tunnel state, given it splits pools into maps and "failed" is currently transient, or does a parity page render pool membership under a different name?
- **Operator surface beyond SAM and the status page** — SOCKS, HTTP proxy, I2PControl/BOB, an interactive console. Undecided, and it interacts with the TUN question.
- **TUN interface** — whether transparent IP-in/IP-out is ever in scope, and what it costs once a SOCKS proxy exists.
- **Event-schema versioning on the cross-node bus** — `i2p_events_forward` has no negotiation, so a router upgrade can silently break a remote subscriber. Real, but not urgent until a second consumer exists.
- **Packaging beyond relx** — deb, static binary, container. 0.2.0 ships the relx tarball; whether that is the right operator artifact is open.
- **0.3.0's shape beyond the two decided tickets** — peer test first, then the Charlie role, then reachability-aware hop selection. The first two are internally sequenced and worth treating as one piece of work. Congestion control and RTT estimation graduated to [#RC68AGE](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/RC68AGE) — **1.0.0 material**, per this map's own Roadmap, which already listed it among the i2pd-parity items. (The fog entry had said 0.3.0; that was wrong.) That gap is why SSU2's per-packet advantage is still only theoretical here: the congestion block is parsed and never acted on.
- **Datagram2 replay protection** — a correctness gap in `i2p_datagram.erl`, not a feature. It fits no pillar and goes unnoticed until someone is replayed at.
- **Addressbook publication** — i2per subscribes to remote addressbooks but never publishes its own `hosts.txt`.
- **Hole punching as a Charlie** — the out-of-session half (HolePunch type 11 to the endpoint Alice signed, then a responder session). Separable from 0.2.0's in-session half, and sharp enough to ticket once that lands. **Carry the spec defect forward:** the Hole Punch section specifies `type :: 7`, but 7 is PeerTest and i2pd uses 11 — implementing the text literally routes a punch into the receiver's peer-test handler.
- **Spec diagram drift, generally** — the SSU2 spec's *diagrams* contradict its own section headings and message table (Hole Punch diagram says 7, heading and table say 11; Peer Test diagram says 10 inside a Type 7 section; Token Request says 6 inside a Type 10 section). The rule established: **read the heading, never the diagram.** Worth a note in `docs/protocol.md` when the Charlie work lands. Two more of the same kind, 2026-10-02: `ssu2.md:3600` says *"See Relay Security above"* and **no such heading exists** (it is Prop 159 at `159-ssu2.md:2104`, the only relay-latency guidance anywhere and purely qualitative), and **there is no hole-punch spec at all** while the transport handbook is a four-line stub — so "the spec is silent on the introducer path" is the state of the documentation, not a gap in anyone's search.
- **Live interop against a Java peer** — the Java Charlie findings are source-level only; i2p-java 0.9.70 at `bb530daa` was read but never built or run. A real interop run is the only way to confirm, and the canonical source mirror is `github.com/i2p/i2p.i2p` (`.i2p` is an I2P-only pseudo-TLD and NXDOMAIN off-net).
- **i2p-java's Charlie and peer-test behaviour** — unverified from this environment (the Java source was unreachable). Half the network runs Java, and the SSU2 spec has no "Processing by Charlie" section, so i2pd is currently the only normative reference. Do not treat i2pd agreement as network agreement.
- **UPnP / NAT-PMP / NatTraversal service** — the one-shot indirect dial exists; the background service does not.

## Out of scope

- **NTCP1, SSU1, I2CP, legacy ElGamal/DSA, Datagram1.** Excluded by the maintainer as the old protocols. Not to be reopened in this effort.
- **Path migration in SSU2.** Past the destination; blocks 18/19 stay keepalive-echo.
- **Deployment, and anything release-composition.** Deployment is a **separate repository** and not part of the core. So: which applications the relx artifact contains, the shipped cookie and distribution policy, and the operator provisioning step are all out of scope here. Concretely, `scripts/build-release.sh` must stop failing the build over `vm.args` distribution or cookie flags — that check is a deployment concern living in the wrong repository.
- **Any GUI, TUI, or HTTP listener in the core.** Decided on [the telemetry contract ticket](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3H11881): the core is data-only, and a presentation app supplies the interface. Note that i2pd and i2p-java both ship a built-in HTTP monitor, so this will look like an omission to anyone comparing them — it is not one.
- **Packaging overhaul.** 0.2.0 ships the existing relx tarball.

## Lane rule, recorded — and it corrects something this map said

**Maintainer's rule: Done means landed, not closed. A ticket stays in Done until its milestone is reached, then that milestone's whole set is closed together. The next milestone is 0.2.0.**

It is now a standing preference in Notes. Recording why it is the right cut: closing at the merge empties Done before anyone has seen the change in a build, and takes the ticket off the board while it is still the thing most worth looking at. Done is the list somebody reads to write release notes and decide whether a release is worth cutting.

**This corrects a claim made here on 2026-10-01.** That comment said the board "carries no ordering information at all" because every ticket sat in Done. The lane assignment was never the problem — holding merged work in Done is exactly what the lane is for. What was missing was *milestone* information, which is a different gap (below).

## The rule splits the board in two, and the split is by tag

| kind | close when |
|---|---|
| **Decision tickets** — `wayfinder:grilling`, `wayfinder:research` | on resolution. Their deliverable is the decision, and Decisions-so-far below indexes closed tickets. |
| **Everything else** — `wayfinder:task` and untagged | at the milestone. |

Recorded because the two kinds are otherwise indistinguishable on the board: a `wayfinder:task` ticket carries a `Solution:` comment and sits in Done, and a resolved `wayfinder:grilling` ticket does the same. Only the tag separates them.

## Three tickets the rule exposes as inconsistent

`#3H11881`, `#1KJMFBH` and `#K84PJ0N` are **resolved decision tickets still open in Done**. All three carry a `Solution:` comment, and all three are already indexed in Decisions-so-far below as closed decisions. `#T3WH4EM` and `#HXT1P2D` — the other two resolved decisions — are correctly closed and on the Closed board.

- **Spec diagram drift, generally** — the SSU2 spec's *diagrams* contradict its own section headings and message table (Hole Punch diagram says 7, heading and table say 11; Peer Test diagram says 10 inside a Type 7 section; Token Request says 6 inside a Type 10 section). The rule established: **read the heading, never the diagram.** Worth a note in `docs/protocol.md` when the Charlie work lands. Two more of the same kind, 2026-10-02: `ssu2.md:3600` says *"See Relay Security above"* and **no such heading exists** (it is Prop 159 at `159-ssu2.md:2104`, the only relay-latency guidance anywhere and purely qualitative), and **there is no hole-punch spec at all** while the transport handbook is a four-line stub — so "the spec is silent on the introducer path" is the state of the documentation, not a gap in anyone's search.
- **Live interop against a Java peer** — the Java Charlie findings are source-level only; i2p-java 0.9.70 at `bb530daa` was read but never built or run. A real interop run is the only way to confirm, and the canonical source mirror is `github.com/i2p/i2p.i2p` (`.i2p` is an I2P-only pseudo-TLD and NXDOMAIN off-net).
- **i2p-java's Charlie and peer-test behaviour** — unverified from this environment (the Java source was unreachable). Half the network runs Java, and the SSU2 spec has no "Processing by Charlie" section, so i2pd is currently the only normative reference. Do not treat i2pd agreement as network agreement.
- **UPnP / NAT-PMP / NatTraversal service** — the one-shot indirect dial exists; the background service does not.

## Out of scope

- **NTCP1, SSU1, I2CP, legacy ElGamal/DSA, Datagram1.** Excluded by the maintainer as the old protocols. Not to be reopened in this effort.
- **Path migration in SSU2.** Past the destination; blocks 18/19 stay keepalive-echo.
- **Deployment, and anything release-composition.** Deployment is a **separate repository** and not part of the core. So: which applications the relx artifact contains, the shipped cookie and distribution policy, and the operator provisioning step are all out of scope here. Concretely, `scripts/build-release.sh` must stop failing the build over `vm.args` distribution or cookie flags — that check is a deployment concern living in the wrong repository.
- **Any GUI, TUI, or HTTP listener in the core.** Decided on [the telemetry contract ticket](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3H11881): the core is data-only, and a presentation app supplies the interface. Note that i2pd and i2p-java both ship a built-in HTTP monitor, so this will look like an omission to anyone comparing them — it is not one.
- **Packaging overhaul.** 0.2.0 ships the existing relx tarball.
